text: Attackers can bypass application logic on dual-use endpoints by omitting mandatory parameters. When multiple operations are handled by a single controller or script, parameter presence acts as an implicit router. Deleting a parameter name or its value can force the backend into unhandled fallback routines, alternative code branches, or privilege escalation paths.

metadata.title: Parameter Omission and Dual-Use Endpoint Exploitation
metadata.technique: Systematic parameter removal across GET, POST, and Cookie headers
execution_steps: Intercept request using an HTTP proxy
Remove one parameter at a time (both key and value)
Submit and inspect response diffs for fallback routing
Trace multi-stage workflows to identify state desynchronization

text: Forced browsing and step skipping in multi-stage workflows allow attackers to reach terminal states without satisfying intermediate requirements. For instance, in two-factor authentication (Login -> 2FA Prompt -> Account Dashboard), directly invoking the post-2FA endpoint via forced browsing circumvents token submission when the server relies on client navigation order instead of server-side state enforcement.

metadata.title: State Sequence Violation and Workflow Step-Skipping
metadata.flawed_assumption: Users will sequentially advance through pages in the order dictated by the client interface.
associated_labs: Authentication bypass via flawed state machine (Practitioner)

text: In e-commerce workflows, state desynchronization occurs when cart adjustment calculations do not recalculate discounts after cart modification. An attacker adds items to exceed a discount threshold (e.g., $1000 for 10% off), applies the coupon, and subsequently removes the items; if the server fails to verify preconditions upon checkout, the discount persists on the smaller total.

metadata.title: State Desynchronization in Post-Condition Order Discounts

rule_constraints.invariant: cart.subtotal >= 1000 must hold at checkout execution

metadata.vulnerability_mechanism: Missing re-validation of pricing invariants when cart mutation occurs in intermediate state.

text: In a purchasing workflow, the client browser transmits the item unit price directly within the POST request payload when adding items to the cart. Because the server fails to validate the price against a database source of truth, an attacker intercepting the request can manipulate the price parameter to an arbitrary low value (e.g., less than available store credit), enabling checkout completion without adequate funds.

metadata.title: Arbitrary Price Tampering via Client-Supplied Parameter
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-602: Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security
attack_steps: Attempt order to determine insufficient credit ceiling.
Tamper 'price' value to an arbitrary lower integer within balance limit.
Submit order via checkout endpoint to complete purchase.
